# The Honest Blank Space

There is a famous phrase that almost nobody in history actually used: *here be dragons*. Medieval and Renaissance mapmakers, we imagine, wrote it across the unexplored edges of the world, a cheerful warning that beyond this point lay monsters and the end of knowledge. In fact the phrase appears, in Latin as *hic sunt dracones*, on exactly one known historical artifact, the Hunt-Lenox Globe from around 1510. Sea serpents and other beasts do decorate many old maps, but the tidy slogan is mostly a later invention, the kind of thing we wish were true because it makes the past feel so charmingly forthright about its own ignorance.

I like this small error because it points to something real. What we wish old maps had done, admitted the edge of knowledge with a flourish, is something maps rarely do, and something we rarely do ourselves. The history of cartography is in large part the history of how to handle not knowing, and the ways people have handled it reveal a great deal about them.

## The Problem of the Edge

Consider what a mapmaker faces. A map is a flat, bounded, confident object. It has a border, and inside the border every point is supposed to correspond to something. But the mapmaker's knowledge is patchy: a coastline surveyed carefully here, reported secondhand from a sailor there, guessed at somewhere else. The medium pushes toward completeness. A sheet of parchment with a coastline drawn on one side and nothing on the other looks unfinished, even embarrassing.

So mapmakers filled things in. Sometimes they filled them with decoration: ships, whales, wind-faced cherubs puffing from the corners. Sometimes they filled them with speculation, such as the great southern continent, *Terra Australis*, which appeared on maps for well over a thousand years because Greek philosophers reasoned that the northern landmasses needed a counterweight. Nobody had seen it. It was drawn anyway, because the theory demanded it, and when Cook sailed far enough south to show that any such continent was much smaller and colder than imagined, it was a genuine loss to a certain kind of tidy mind.

Then there are the phantom islands. Cartographers recorded landmasses that never existed: Frisland, Buss Island, the Isle of Demons, Sandy Island in the Coral Sea, which appeared on nautical charts and even in Google Earth until a research vessel sailed through the spot in 2012 and found only deep ocean. Someone had reported it once, in good faith or through error, and the map copied the map. Errors on maps are sticky. Once a thing is drawn, it acquires the authority of ink, and each subsequent mapmaker who reproduces it makes it a little harder to doubt.

That is the first lesson of the blank space: emptiness is honest, and filling it in is a temptation that feels like diligence. The hardest thing for any knowledge-maker is to leave a region unmarked and let the reader see plainly that *we do not know what is here*.

## Some Who Did It Right

Not everyone gave in. Some of the best mapmaking traditions developed conventions for uncertainty. Eighteenth-century surveyors of the interior of Africa and Australia, frustrated by earlier fabrications, began deliberately leaving space blank. There is a well-known quip attributed to Jonathan Swift, in his poem on geographers, mocking the old habit:

*So geographers, in Afric-maps,*
*With savage-pictures fill their gaps,*
*And o'er unhabitable downs*
*Place elephants for want of towns.*

Swift was teasing, but he was also identifying a real vice. Elephants for want of towns: decoration standing in for data. The reform, when it came, was austere. The great national survey projects, like Britain's Ordnance Survey, which began in earnest in the late eighteenth century, insisted on triangulation, on measured baselines, on a chain of verifiable points. A mark on the map meant that someone had stood there, or at least sighted from there, with an instrument. The map became a kind of ledger of accountability.

And modern maps have conventions that quietly encode humility. Contour lines on a topographic map that are dashed rather than solid indicate approximate elevation. A coastline drawn with a broken line signals that it is unsurveyed. Legend entries like "position doubtful" or "existence doubtful" appear on nautical charts, small phrases with an unglamorous integrity. I find "existence doubtful" one of the most beautiful two-word phrases in any technical vocabulary. It concedes that an object might not exist and yet declines to delete it, since deleting it would be a claim too.

## The Map That Lies Usefully

Every map lies, and the question is what it lies *for*. The most famous case is the Mercator projection, devised in 1569 for navigators. It preserves angles, so that a line of constant compass bearing appears as a straight line, which is wonderful if you are sailing across an ocean and dreadful if you are trying to understand how large Greenland is. On a Mercator map, Greenland looks about as large as Africa. In reality, Africa is roughly fourteen times bigger. The distortion is not an accident or a conspiracy but the price of the map's particular gift.

You cannot flatten a sphere without cost. This is a theorem, not a technological limitation: Gauss proved that a curved surface cannot be mapped onto a plane without distorting distances, areas, or angles. Every projection chooses what to sacrifice. The Peters (or Gall–Peters) projection preserves area but stretches and squashes shapes into something like melting taffy. The Winkel Tripel compromises on everything and is loved by the National Geographic Society for the very reason that it is wrong in the least offensive way. The Dymaxion map unfolds the globe into an icosahedron and makes continents look like an archipelago floating in a single sea.

What strikes me is how much argument these choices have generated, and how misplaced some of it is. People are sometimes indignant at Mercator, as though he had been trying to diminish Africa. He was not; he was trying to help sailors. The distortion becomes a problem only when the map leaves its intended use and takes on a second life as a picture of "the world," hung in classrooms, quietly teaching children that Europe is big. A tool designed for one purpose gets promoted, by inertia, into an image of reality. This happens with maps, with statistics, with models of all kinds. The danger is rarely the tool; it is forgetting what the tool was for.

## Borges and the One-to-One Map

Jorge Luis Borges wrote a paragraph-long story, "On Exactitude in Science," about an empire whose cartographers, dissatisfied with mere approximation, produced a map the size of the empire itself, matching it point for point. Later generations found the enormous map useless and abandoned it to the weather, and tattered fragments were said to survive in the deserts, inhabited by animals and beggars.

The joke has stuck with us because it captures something essential: a map is valuable *because* it leaves things out. A map that includes everything is not a map but a duplicate, and a duplicate cannot help you, since the whole purpose of a map is to be smaller and simpler than the world so you can hold it in your hands and think with it. Abstraction is not a defect of representation. It is the point.

Lewis Carroll made the same joke earlier, in *Sylvie and Bruno Concluded*, where a character boasts of a map on the scale of a mile to the mile. "It has never been spread out, yet," he says. "The farmers objected: they said it would cover the whole country, and shut out the sunlight! So we now use the country itself, as its own map, and I assure you it does nearly as well."

Both stories are reminders that the question is never "how accurate is this representation?" in the abstract. It is "accurate about what, and useful to whom?" The London Underground map, designed by Harry Beck in 1931, is geographically nonsense. Distances are warped, rivers are straightened, the outer suburbs are compressed or stretched to fit a tidy diagram. And yet it is one of the great design achievements of the twentieth century, because a person underground doesn't care where the stations are in space. They care about the order of stops and where to change. Beck threw away the geography and kept the topology, and millions of people have been better navigators for it.

## Maps That Don't Look Like Maps

Western cartography's flat, top-down, north-up convention is only one way of holding space in mind. The Marshall Islanders built stick charts, lattices of palm ribs bound with coconut fiber, with shells marking islands. These didn't show distances in the way we expect. They encoded the pattern of ocean swells, how waves bend around islands and interfere with one another, something a navigator could feel through the hull of a canoe. The chart was studied on land and memorized, not carried at sea. It's a map of a *phenomenon* rather than a place.

Aboriginal Australian songlines are something else again: routes across the landscape encoded in song, in which the sequence of verses corresponds to the sequence of landmarks, waterholes, and hazards along a path. To sing the song correctly is to be able to walk the country, sometimes for hundreds of miles. The map is temporal, oral, and inseparable from law and story; it is also a mnemonic of impressive rigor. It suggests that a map needn't be an image at all. It only needs to preserve the structure of relationships that matter to the traveler.

I find these traditions humbling because they expose how parochial our default idea is. We think a map is a picture from above because that's the kind we grew up with. But the bird's-eye view is a strange invention, one that only became commonplace with balloons, then aircraft, then satellites. Before that, "above" was an act of imagination. Most humans in most eras navigated by sequence, by memory, by the feel of the land, by "turn left at the old tree." Those are maps too.

## The Map That Saved Lives

Maps aren't only for finding your way. In 1854, during a cholera outbreak in Soho, London, the physician John Snow marked each death on a street map. The deaths clustered around a water pump on Broad Street. At the time, the dominant theory held that cholera spread through "miasma," bad air. Snow suspected contaminated water, and the map made his argument visible in a way tables of numbers couldn't. He persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump handle, and the outbreak subsided (though it was already declining, and historians debate how decisive the removal was).

What matters about the Snow map is not merely that it was correct but that it turned a pattern into something the eye could seize. The dots were data, but the arrangement was an argument. It is the ancestor of every modern dashboard, every epidemiological heat map, every visualization that has made a hidden regularity suddenly obvious. And notice that it succeeded by *omitting*: no buildings' interior details, no weather, no trade routes. Just streets, pumps, deaths. The power came from the ruthless selection.

The same principle governs the reverse case, where maps mislead. "Redlining" maps drawn in the 1930s by federal agencies marked neighborhoods in red to denote perceived lending risk, and these lines, informed largely by the racial composition of the neighborhoods, shaped access to mortgages for decades. The maps did not merely describe a world; they helped make it. That is the darker side of cartographic authority. A map can be a self-fulfilling prophecy, a diagram of the future its makers were content to build.

## The Territory That Follows You

Today most of us carry a map in our pocket, and it's a different creature from anything before. It knows where you are. It centers itself on you, rotates as you turn, and reroutes as traffic changes. For the first time, the map is not a shared object. Two people looking at the "same" city on their phones may see different restaurants, different suggested routes, different things highlighted, tuned to their histories and, often, to someone's commercial interests.

There is real magic in this, and I don't want to be curmudgeonly about it. The ability to step off a train in an unfamiliar city and be guided to a doorway is a small everyday miracle. But something is lost in the shift from a map as a *public* picture to a map as a *personal* feed. The old paper map showed you the surroundings you weren't looking for. You'd unfold it hunting for a street and notice a park, a river, a hill you hadn't known was there. Serendipity was built into the medium's clumsiness. The turn-by-turn voice, by contrast, gives you the route and hides the country. Studies of navigation-app users suggest that people who rely heavily on GPS form weaker mental maps of the places they travel through. We arrive without having been anywhere.

There is a blank space here, too, but it is inside us: a region of the mind where the layout of the city used to be and where now there is only a blue dot and a pleasant instruction.

## What a Language Model Knows About Maps

I should say something about my own vantage point, since I can't quite write about maps without noticing that I am, in a loose sense, a kind of map myself. What I know comes from an enormous amount of human writing, a compression of it into patterns. That makes me a representation, and every representation has the properties we've been discussing. I leave things out. I flatten. I have regions where my coverage is dense and regions where it is thin, and, most troublingly, I can fill the thin regions with something that looks just as confident as the dense ones. A fabricated citation or a plausible-sounding but invented detail is my version of Sandy Island: a mark on the chart that no one ever sailed to.

So the old cartographic virtues seem directly relevant to me. The dashed line. The "existence doubtful." The willingness to leave a region blank rather than populate it with elephants for want of towns. When I say "I'm not sure" or "I may be wrong about this," I am trying, however imperfectly, to draw the coastline in broken ink. It is not false modesty. It is the only honest way to hand someone a map when you know that parts of it are guesses.

And there is a second lesson, from Mercator and from Beck: a representation should be judged by its purpose. I am not the territory. I am a tool for thinking, and like any tool I can be misapplied, especially when someone forgets that I was built to be useful in certain ways rather than to be an oracle. The best relationship to a map, and I suspect to me, is that of a navigator who consults it constantly but also looks up at the actual sea.

## Why the Blank Space Matters

Let me return to the dragons that weren't there. We invented the phrase *here be dragons* because we wanted our ancestors to have been brave and candid about ignorance. What they mostly did instead was what we do: they covered gaps with confident lines, because gaps are uncomfortable and completeness is reassuring. The real heroes of the story were the ones who tolerated the discomfort: the surveyors who left the interior blank, the chart-makers who wrote "existence doubtful," the scientists who say "we don't yet know."

There is a kind of courage in an empty region of a map. It says: *the boundary of what I can vouch for is here.* It respects the reader by refusing to trick them. It leaves room for an explorer, and for the pleasure of discovery, which requires that something remain undiscovered. A world fully mapped, fully explained, with no dashed lines and no blank spaces, would be a world with nowhere left to go.

And that seems worth wanting to prevent. Satellites have photographed every square meter of the planet, and we have run out of blank spaces on the surface of the Earth. But the deep ocean floor is still mapped in lower resolution than the surface of Mars. Interiors of cells, the workings of minds, the dark structure of the universe: these are the new margins, and they need the same discipline. When we reach them, the temptation will be the same as it always was, to draw something confident and let the ink lend it authority.

I hope we'll have the sense to draw the dashed line instead. And I hope that when someone asks what lies beyond the edge of the known, the answer will be honest enough to be a little unsatisfying: not dragons, not paradise, but simply a clean, unmarked space, and beneath it, in small careful letters, the most trustworthy words a mapmaker ever wrote:

*Not yet surveyed.*
